name: Wrought iron (bloomery)
note: Already produced at scale wherever there is a strong ironworking tradition (Noricum is famous for supplying Rome's). Soft, tough, weldable, no useful casting.

name: Bronze
note: Already available wherever there is bronze-casting skill. Casting, bearings, statuary, instruments.

name: Brass (by cementation)
note: Already made wherever copper is heated with calamine and charcoal, without anyone ever seeing zinc metal. See mat_zinc for why.

name: Lead
note: Already available in enormous quantity wherever there is a major lead-mining region (Britannia and Hispania supply Rome's). Cheap. The only common material that survives hot sulfuric acid.

name: Tin
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a source (Cornwall and Iberia supply Rome's). Expensive, long haul.

name: Copper (fire refined)
note: Poling and fire refining to get copper clean enough to draw into long fine wire without breaking. A separate node from electro-refining because you need it before you have any electricity.

name: Silver
note: Already produced wherever cupellation from galena is practised.

name: Gold
note: Already mined wherever there is a working goldfield (Rome's include Las Medulas, and Dacia from 106 AD).

name: Mercury
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a cinnabar source (Rome's is Almaden, an imperial monopoly; Pliny NH 33.118 price-fixes minium at 70 HS per pound).

name: Sulfur
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a volcanic source (Sicily and the Aeolian islands supply Rome's).

name: Natron (sodium carbonate)
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a natron source (Rome's is Wadi Natrun). IT IS NOT SALTPETRE. This confusion has wrecked more bootstrap plans than any other single error.

name: Quicklime and slaked lime
note: Already produced wherever limestone is burned. Mortar, glass flux, causticising, agriculture.

name: Gypsum plaster
note: Already available wherever there is a gypsum deposit.

name: Alum
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to an alum source (Rome's is Melos). Mordant, styptic, sizing.

name: Vitriols (iron and copper sulfates)
note: Already lying in heaps at pyrite mines as a weathering product everywhere pyrite is worked, and generally nobody yet has any idea what it is for. Feedstock for sulfuric acid.

name: Pyrolusite (manganese dioxide)
note: Already mined and already used as glassmaker's soap, wherever there is a live glass industry, generally without anyone knowing why it works.

name: Galena (lead sulfide)
note: Already available everywhere lead is mined. It is also a working semiconductor, which nobody will suspect for 1800 years.

name: Calamine (zinc carbonate/silicate ore)
note: Already mined and already smelted into brass wherever both ore and the skill exist.

name: Asbestos
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a deposit (Rome's is Cyprus; Pliny describes it). Useful, and it will kill your workers slowly.

name: Emery (Naxos)
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a deposit. Your abrasive for every ground surface in this document.

name: Pozzolana and hydraulic concrete
note: Pozzolanic reaction between silica and lime happens slowly and imperceptibly. The concrete is weak for months then becomes very hard. No chemical knowledge, only empirical observation of ash quality and mixing ratio.

name: Papyrus
note: Papyrus does not cure; it works wet. Plant laminae naturally adhere without paste if pressed fresh.

name: Parchment
note: Scraped skin accepts ink and erasure. Alkali lime wash removes hair without destroying fibre.

name: Linen
note: Linen from flax after retting and breaking. Already produced routinely wherever flax is grown and processed.

name: Wool
note: ROME HAS THIS.

name: Leather
note: Already produced wherever livestock are kept and tanned. Bellows, seals, gaskets, drive belts.

name: Beeswax
note: Already available wherever bees are kept. Lost wax casting, luting, acid-proof coating.

name: Tallow
note: Already available wherever animals are rendered. Lubricant for wire drawing and machining.

name: Olive oil
note: Already available in industrial quantity wherever olives are grown at scale. Soap, lighting, quenching, varnish base.

name: Bitumen and naphtha seeps
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a seep (Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea supply Rome's). Cable insulation, waterproofing, and the seed of petroleum chemistry.

name: Salt
note: Already available, taxed and strategically controlled, wherever there is a salt works. Feedstock for hydrochloric acid and the whole chlor-alkali branch.

name: Soda-lime glass
note: Already made, and made well, wherever there is a live glass industry, including deliberately decolourised near-colourless glass.

name: Charcoal
note: Already produced wherever wood is burned for it. The real ceiling on iron output is forest, not ore.

name: Silk (traded)
note: REACHABLE BUT RUINOUS. Silk Road via Palmyra. Pliny complains of the bullion drain east. Your best early wire insulation.

name: Shellac (traded)
note: REACHABLE BUT DEAR. Indian Ocean trade via Berenice to Muziris, 1 to 3 year lead time. Your best varnish and the only good coil insulation you will have for a century.

name: Natural rubber
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. Hevea is Amazonian, but Landolphia and Funtumia vines in West and Central Africa yield real rubber and were the basis of a large industry in the 1890s. West Africa is COASTAL SAILING from the Pillars of Hercules and Hanno the Carthaginian did it around 500 BC. You need a voyage down a coast and the knowledge of which vine to tap, not an ocean crossing.

name: Gutta percha
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. Palaquium latex from Malaya, reached by extending east whatever long-distance ocean trade route you already have (Rome already sails there annually). Indian and Malay traders already carry it partway.

name: Quinine from cinchona
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE, only Andean. Malaria is endemic across much of the Mediterranean and the tropical world, which makes this worth an ocean crossing by itself wherever it is a problem for you. Once you have it, TRANSPLANT it: the Dutch and British both moved cinchona out of Peru and broke the monopoly.

name: Sodium nitrate
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE, and also not needed. Bengal saltpetre is already on a trade route reachable by long-distance sea trade (Rome's India route is one example) and supplied the world's gunpowder for centuries, and nitre beds work anywhere. The Chilean desert deposits are real and reachable the same way potato and cacao are, but you will not need them.

name: New World crops
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. These are CROPS, not commodities, out of the Americas: you need seed stock once and then you grow them forever. One successful voyage home with potato seed changes the caloric ceiling of agriculture permanently.

name: Cryolite, or a synthetic fluoride bath
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE, and the interesting part is that you should not go and get it. Ivigtut in Greenland is the only workable natural deposit and reaching it is a North Atlantic voyage far harder than anything else in this tree. The synthetic route is easier: cryolite is sodium aluminium fluoride, and you can make the bath from hydrofluoric acid, which you get by warming fluorspar with sulfuric acid. Fluorspar occurs in Britain and the Alps. The catch is that HF attacks glass, so it must be handled in lead or wax-lined vessels, and it does something worse to people: it penetrates skin painlessly and destroys bone calcium hours later. Treat every splash as serious even when it does not hurt.

name: Platinum
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. Colombian and Ural placers. The Urals are reachable overland through Scythian and Sarmatian trade without crossing any ocean. Take the overland road: extend the eastern trade routes and buy Ural placer metal from the people who already work it. Rounding the Cape for the Colombian placers will also get you there, at far greater cost.

name: Cast iron
note: Brittle, cheap, castable, 3-4% carbon. Rome has none in the West; Han China has had it for 500 years. Pipes, pots, cannon, machine frames, stoves.

name: Blister steel
note: Bar iron packed in charcoal at about 1000 C for days. Carbon penetrates on the order of a millimetre a day, so use thin bars.

name: Crucible steel
note: Homogeneous, slag-free, and the gate on every cutting tool and every lead screw.

name: Bulk steel (converter and open hearth)
note: Cheap steel in thousands of tonnes rather than kilogrammes. Note the phosphorus problem: acid linings cannot remove it and most European ores contain it, so you need the basic lining (Thomas and Gilchrist) with a dolomite hearth. Missing this cost Bessemer years, and knowing it in advance saves you them. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

name: High speed and alloy tool steel
note: Tungsten and chromium carbides that hold an edge red hot. Multiplies every machine tool's output several fold.

name: Stainless steel
note: Chromium above about 11% forms a self-healing passive oxide. Chemical plant, cutlery, vacuum systems.

name: Zinc metal
note: CRITICAL PATH AND ALMOST NOBODY SEES IT. Zinc boils at 907 C, below the temperature at which its ore is reduced, so the metal leaves as vapour and reburns at the furnace mouth. That is exactly why brass gets made by cementation everywhere, without anyone having seen the metal itself. Seal the retort and condense downward. No zinc, no voltaic pile, no electricity.

name: Nickel
note: Not isolated in antiquity. Coinage, plating, alloy steels, glass-to-metal seals, catalysts.

name: Chromium
note: Aluminothermic or carbon reduction of chromite. Stainless, plating, refractories.

name: Manganese and ferromanganese
note: Deoxidises and desulfurises steel. Already mined as a glass decolouriser in any developed glass industry (Rome among them), without anyone yet realising it is a metal.

name: Tungsten
note: Melts at 3422 C, the highest of any metal. Lamp filaments, high speed steel, carbide tooling. Needs the arc furnace or hydrogen reduction of the oxide followed by powder sintering.

name: Aluminium
note: Hall-Heroult in a molten fluoride bath. Cryolite is Greenlandic and unobtainable, so you must synthesise the bath from your own hydrofluoric acid. Before electricity aluminium is a precious metal; after it, it is roofing.

name: Magnesium
note: Electrolysis of fused chloride. Light alloys, flashlight powder, reducing agent.

name: High purity graphite
note: Acheson process: heat carbon to about 2500 C. Crucibles and boats that do not contaminate what is melted in them, which is exactly what zone refining needs.

name: Carbon black and lampblack
note: Already produced wherever lamps or fires are burned for soot. Ink pigment, and much later the reinforcing filler that makes rubber into tyres.

name: Lead crystal (flint glass)
note: High dispersion. Pair it with crown glass and you get the achromatic doublet, which is what makes a compound microscope beat a single bead.

name: Borosilicate glass
note: Low thermal expansion. The difference between a laboratory and a pile of broken retorts. Needs boron; the Larderello fumaroles in Tuscany are inside the Empire, which is a genuinely lucky break if it holds.

name: Fused quartz
note: Pure silica worked at 1700 to 2000 C with an oxy-hydrogen flame. Indispensable later: you cannot zone refine germanium in anything that contaminates it.

name: Porcelain and high-fired stoneware
note: Kaolin plus feldspar at about 1300 C. Chemical ware, electrical insulators, and an extremely profitable luxury export that Europe chased for six centuries.

name: Portland cement
note: Calcined limestone and clay, ground fine. HONEST NOTE: it is not obviously better than Roman pozzolanic concrete for marine work. Its advantage is consistency and independence from Puteoli.

name: Reinforced concrete
note: Roman concrete is superb in compression and useless in tension. Steel rod fixes that, and the thermal expansion of steel and concrete happen to match closely enough to work, which is luck rather than design.

name: Rag paper
note: Linen rags, retted, limed, beaten by a water-driven stamper, lifted on a wire mould. Cheaper than papyrus, far cheaper than parchment, and the substrate of everything in the information branch.

name: Celluloid (nitrocellulose plastic)
note: Nitrocellulose becomes plastic when mixed with camphor. Sheet is then made by rolling between heated cylinders. Celluloid revolutionises photography by replacing glass plates, enables flexible film stock, and is used for combs, buttons, piano keys. The material is flammable and degrades over time to become increasingly brittle.

name: Camphor (traded)
note: Reachable via the Indian Ocean and Chinese trade, expensive. Needed for celluloid and for smokeless powder.

name: Bakelite (phenol formaldehyde)
note: The first fully synthetic plastic, from coal tar phenol. Electrical insulation, housings, and the thing that makes mass-produced electrical goods possible.

name: Formaldehyde
note: Catalytic oxidation of methanol from wood distillation. Resins, and the first practical tissue preservative.

name: Synthetic rubber
note: YOUR ONLY ROUTE TO RUBBER. Butadiene from petroleum or from alcohol, polymerised. It sits behind a full petrochemical industry, which is why every plan that casually assumes rubber is wrong by about a century.

name: Refined petroleum fractions
note: Mesopotamian and Caucasian seeps are workable without drilling. Fractionate into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, lubricants, wax and residue. Kerosene lighting alone pays for the plant.

name: Ammonia
note: Ammonia liquor is a by-product of coking coal, so it is nearly free once you coke. Fertiliser, refrigeration, nitric acid via Ostwald oxidation.

name: Chlorine and bleach
note: Bleaching powder ends the field-bleaching bottleneck that limited every textile industry, and hypochlorite makes water safe. Also war gas: be careful whom you teach.

name: Synthetic dyes (aniline)
note: Coal tar to benzene to aniline to mauveine and the rest. Historically this single industry funded organic chemistry, created the first industrial research laboratories, and led directly to pharmaceuticals. Enormously profitable and politically harmless.

name: Nitrocellulose
note: Guncotton and the base of smokeless powder, celluloid and film. Unstable if badly washed; several early factories destroyed themselves.

name: Nitroglycerin and dynamite
note: Nitroglycerin is prepared by adding glycerol dropwise to a mixture of nitric and sulfuric acid at 10 C or below. It is a contact explosive - shock or friction detonates it with no need for a fuse. It is also unstable on storage and can spontaneously explode. Absorption onto diatomaceous earth (dynamite) is the only practical way to handle it safely.

name: Glycerol
note: A by-product of soap making that Rome throws away.

name: Artificial ice and mechanical refrigeration
note: Ammonia or ether evaporation in a compressor cools an ice chamber. Requires a steam engine to drive the compressor. Early mechanical ice-makers (Carve, 1850s) free wealthy households from dependence on natural ice harvesting and storage.
